slides.say: A new app is downloaded five times on day one. On every later day, it is downloaded twice as many times as on the day before. How many times is it downloaded in total through day n?

So they ask for a formula, and there's an n in every choice. That's the second kind of pattern, a sequence. We don't use school formulas here. [short pause] We'll plug in a number for n, and check the choices.
at: So they ask for a formula

slides.say: [short pause] Let's plug in n is three. Why did we pick three? Because it's small, so the days are easy to write out. And it's big enough to keep the choices apart. In a minute we'll see why not one.
Day one is five downloads. Every later day is twice the day before. So day two is ten, and day three is twenty.
The total through day three is five plus ten plus twenty. Five plus ten is fifteen. Fifteen plus twenty is thirty-five. So the right choice must give thirty-five when n is three.

Choice number one is five times the difference, two to the power of n, minus one. Let's put in three. Two to the power of three is eight, and eight minus one is seven. Five times seven is thirty-five. It works.
at: Two to the power of three

slides.say: Choice number two is five n squared. Three squared is nine. Five times nine is forty-five. That's not thirty-five, so choice number two is out.
at: so choice number two is out

slides.say: Choice number three is two to the power of n, plus five. Eight plus five is thirteen, so choice number three is out.
Choice number four is five times two to the power of n. Five times eight is forty, so it's out too. Only choice number one gives thirty-five, so choice number one is our answer.
at: so choice number one is our answer

slides.say: Why not plug in n is one? It's quicker, so let's see what happens. Through day one, the total is just five.

Choice number one gives five times one, because two minus one is one. That's five. Choice number two gives five times one squared, also five. Choice number three gives two plus five, seven. Choice number four gives five times two, ten. So two choices survive, and we'd need another number anyway.

That's how these questions are often built. Plugging in one leaves two choices standing. Three is small enough to calculate, and big enough to separate the choices. And if two choices still survive with three, plug in four as well. Choice number one is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
